entry.title: From Agents to Understanding
entry.content:
What if an AI system could describe not only what it should do, but what it is trying to understand?

AI agents are rapidly becoming capable of planning, calling tools, delegating work, maintaining state, inspecting results, and iterating until a task reaches a stopping point.

A simplified agent loop looks like this:

That model is extraordinarily useful. But it is primarily organized around action.

There is another question worth exploring:

What would an AI-native architecture look like if understanding itself became a first-class computational object?

Not understanding hidden inside model weights. Not understanding implied by a final paragraph. But understanding that can be structured, traced, questioned, projected, revised, and acted upon.

This is the territory explored by HOLOFLUX, IOP, and COSMOS.

1. From execution to inquiry

A conventional agent can be represented conceptually as:

agent :researcher do
  goal :answer_question

  plan
  select_tool
  execute
  evaluate
  repeat
end

Its central question is:

What should I do next?

An inquiry-oriented system introduces another question before action:

What is actually happening here?

intent :understand do
  observe :what_is

  expose :assumptions
  expose :contradictions

  preserve :unknowns
  preserve :uncertainty

  allow :insight

  act_from :understanding
end

The movement becomes:

Action remains important. It is simply no longer the only organizing principle.

2. The missing epistemic layer

Consider concepts that frequently become mixed together inside AI-generated answers:

Reference
Source
Source Passage
Observation
Claim
Evidence
Hypothesis
Contradiction
Uncertainty
Understanding

They are related, but they are not interchangeable:

Citation ≠ Source
Source ≠ Evidence
Evidence ≠ Claim
Claim ≠ Understanding
Operational Success ≠ Epistemic Acceptance

A model successfully retrieving a document does not establish the claims contained in that document. A source asserting something does not automatically turn the assertion into evidence. A generated explanation does not automatically become understanding.

What if those distinctions became part of the runtime?

3. A practical case: the Grebennikov inquiry

Viktor S. Grebennikov was an entomologist and naturalist whose book My World includes a chapter describing what he called the Cavity Structural Effect (CSE) and extraordinary claims involving antigravitational phenomena.

The purpose of using this case is not to assert that antigravity was demonstrated. It is useful precisely because it forces an inquiry system to keep source, observation, interpretation, evidence, contradiction, and unknowns separate.

A weak summarization pipeline can collapse the semantic layers into something like:

Grebennikov discovered an antigravity effect associated with insect structures.

An inquiry-oriented representation keeps the distinctions visible:

Grebennikov reported observation X.
Grebennikov interpreted X as effect Y.
He proposed mechanism Z.
Independent confirmation is a separate question.
Alternative explanations remain possible.
The claim cannot be treated as established merely because it appears in the primary source.

4. Starting with intent

Instead of beginning with:

task :summarize_grebennikov

we can begin with:

intent :understand_antigravity_claim

A task such as summarize already specifies an output. An intent such as understand defines a purpose while leaving the conclusion open.

intent :understand_antigravity_claim do
  preserve :unknown
  avoid :premature_conclusion
  avoid :confusing_claim_with_evidence
end

The system has not been asked to prove Grebennikov correct or wrong. It has been asked to understand what can actually be concluded.

5. Context is more than a prompt

context do
  include :grebennikov_primary_source
  include :reported_observations
  include :known_physics
  include :independent_sources
  include :replication_history
end

Context can itself have structure:

The primary source can become an explicit object:

reference :grebennikov_primary_source do
  author "Viktor S. Grebennikov"
  work "My World"
  chapter 5
  title "The Natural Phenomena of AntiGravitation and Invisibility in Insects due to the Grebennikov Cavity Structure Effect"
  source_type :book_chapter
  language :english_translation
  url "https://geomagnetics.org/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/myworldbyviktorgrebennikovfinpdf.pdf"
end

The reference is now part of the semantic model rather than merely an item in a bibliography.

6. Epistemic policies

Before asking the system to investigate anything, we can describe the rules under which knowledge may be constructed:

policies do
  distinguish :observation, :claim
  distinguish :claim, :evidence
  distinguish :source, :evidence
  distinguish :hypothesis, :demonstrated_mechanism

  preserve :provenance
  preserve :contradiction
  preserve :uncertainty
  preserve :unknown
end

These are not merely security guardrails. They are epistemic guardrails.

policy :claim_acceptance do
  require :supporting_evidence
  preserve :contradictory_evidence
  preserve :source_identity
  prohibit :source_as_evidence_by_default
end

7. HOLOFLUX: making the semantic field explicit

A compact formulation is:

HOLOFLUX = Meaning + Explication

Applied to the Grebennikov case:

holoflux :grebennikov_field do

  source :grebennikov_my_world do
    reference :grebennikov_primary_source
    author "Viktor S. Grebennikov"
    chapter 5
  end

  observation :o1 do
    statement "Certain insect structures were reported as having unusual microscopic geometries."
    provenance do
      source :grebennikov_my_world
      location :chapter_5
    end
  end

  claim :c1 do
    statement "Cavity structures produce a distinct physical effect."
    asserted_by :grebennikov
    provenance do
      source :grebennikov_my_world
      location :chapter_5
    end
  end

  claim :c2 do
    statement "The proposed effect can produce antigravitational behavior."
    asserted_by :grebennikov
    depends_on :c1
    provenance do
      source :grebennikov_my_world
      location :chapter_5
    end
  end

  evidence :e1 do
    supports :c2
    status :insufficient
    provenance do
      source :grebennikov_my_world
      kind :reported_experience
    end
  end

  unknown :u1 do
    asks "Is there an independently reproducible anomalous force?"
  end

  unknown :u2 do
    asks "Can the reported phenomenon be experimentally distinguished from known physical effects?"
  end

  uncertainty :high
end

The prose has become a semantic field that can be inspected without collapsing observation, claim, evidence, unknown, and uncertainty into one statement.

8. IOP: inquiry without a predetermined conclusion

IOP = Intent + Understanding

Intent here does not mean produce answer X. It defines the mode of inquiry.

inquiry :antigravity_claim do
  observe :reported_phenomena
  observe :measurement_quality
  observe :replication_status
  observe :alternative_explanations

  preserve :unknown

  do_not_assume :claim_is_true
  do_not_assume :claim_is_false

  ask "What is actually demonstrated?"
  ask "What remains interpretation?"
  ask "What observation could discriminate between competing explanations?"
end

The conclusion does not need to be forced.

9. allow, not produce

produce :insight

implies that insight is mechanically generated from a command. An inquiry-oriented DSL can instead say:

emergence :insight do
  conditions :attention,
             :observation,
             :sufficient_context
  commanded false
end

or:

inquiry :understand do
  observe :what_is
  preserve :contradiction
  preserve :unknown
  remain_with :question
  allow :insight
end

This introduces an important distinction:

cause ≠ condition ≠ emergence

10. Understanding is not the output

Suppose the inquiry reaches this state:

The primary source reports an antigravity interpretation of an alleged phenomenon.
The existence of the source establishes that the claim was made.
It does not by itself establish that the proposed physical mechanism is valid.
Independent reproducibility therefore remains a central unresolved question.

That understanding can produce several outputs.

The outputs are projections. They are not the understanding itself.

11. COSMOS as the orchestration layer

COSMOS coordinates the whole:

COSMOS = Orchestration of the Whole


cosmos :grebennikov_inquiry do

  reference :primary_source do
    author "Viktor S. Grebennikov"
    work "My World"
    chapter 5
    title "The Natural Phenomena of AntiGravitation and Invisibility in Insects due to the Grebennikov Cavity Structure Effect"
    source_type :book_chapter
    language :english_translation
    url "https://geomagnetics.org/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/myworldbyviktorgrebennikovfinpdf.pdf"
  end

  intent :understand_antigravity_claim do
    preserve :unknown
    avoid :premature_conclusion
    avoid :confusing_claim_with_evidence
  end

  context do
    include reference(:primary_source)
    include :reported_observations
    include :known_physics
    include :independent_sources
    include :replication_history
  end

  policies do
    distinguish :observation, :claim
    distinguish :claim, :evidence
    distinguish :source, :evidence
    distinguish :hypothesis, :demonstrated_mechanism

    preserve :provenance
    preserve :contradiction
    preserve :uncertainty
  end

  capabilities do
    use :retrieval
    use :source_validation
    use :holoflux
    use :iop
    use :diagram_generation
  end

  orchestrate do
    acquire :sources

    delegate :semantic_explication,
             to: :holoflux

    delegate :inquiry,
             to: :iop

    integrate :understanding
  end

  project do
    as :dsl
    as :mermaid
    as :epistemic_report
  end
end

The DSL describes:

Intent
Context
Policies
Capabilities
Orchestration
Understanding
Projection

It describes the epistemic architecture of the system.

12. From DSL to Mermaid

Because the semantic model is explicit, it can also be projected as a diagram:

The important part is not the visual alone. The diagram and the textual explanation come from the same semantic structure.

13. Implicate and explicate

The architecture suggests an analogy with David Bohm’s distinction between implicate and explicate order. This is a conceptual analogy, not a claim that the runtime implements Bohm’s physical theory.

A text contains more possible meaning than any one representation of it. Relationships, tensions, assumptions, interpretations, perspectives, and unanswered questions remain partially enfolded.

A DSL can then be seen as one explicit projection:

The resulting semantic field can then be projected as a DSL, diagram, narrative, or behavior without confusing any one projection with the whole.

The DSL is therefore not the implicate order itself. It is an explication of part of it.

14. From documentation to executable architecture

At first, this DSL can serve as architectural documentation. The more interesting possibility is that it eventually becomes executable.

cosmos :research_system do
  intent :understand_article

  policies do
    preserve :unknown
    preserve :provenance
  end

  capabilities do
    use :retrieval
    use :holoflux
    use :iop
  end
end

A runtime could resolve use :retrieval into search, RAG, vector storage, an MCP server, a knowledge graph, or an agent. COSMOS deals with capabilities; the runtime deals with implementation.

15. Agent behavior can become part of the DSL

agent :researcher do
  behavior :investigate_claim do
    receive :claim
    retrieve :sources
    preserve :provenance

    distinguish :source,
                :evidence,
                :claim

    detect :contradictions
    assess :uncertainty

    open :inquiry,
         when: :unknown_remains

    emit :understanding
  end
end

That leads to a richer model of computation:

Entity
= Meaning
+ State
+ Behavior
+ Relations
+ Transitions
+ Constraints
+ Emergence

and a richer AI-native system:

Intent
+ Context
+ Semantic Field
+ Behavior
+ Inquiry
+ Understanding
+ Projection

16. From agentic systems to inquiry-oriented systems

Chatbot

Agent

Inquiry-Oriented AI-Native System

This does not make conventional agents obsolete. It adds another layer.

The agent asks:

What should I do next?

The epistemic runtime can also ask:

What do we actually know?

Why do we think we know it?

What contradicts it?

What remains unknown?

What conclusion is justified?

17. A Krishnamurti-inspired semantics of inquiry

The language of IOP draws inspiration from concepts often explored by J. Krishnamurti:

observation
conditioning
conflict
attention
ending
insight
intelligence

The purpose is not to turn those concepts into a deterministic algorithm. Instead, they suggest another vocabulary for computational inquiry:

intent :understand do
  not :control
  not :premature_conclusion

  observe :what_is
  preserve :unknown
  remain_with :question

  allow :insight
end

The distinction between produce :insight and allow :insight is intentional. The first describes command. The second describes conditions under which something may emerge.

18. What the Grebennikov example reveals

The antigravity case is useful precisely because it prevents the system from taking an easy path.

An AI could simply say:

Grebennikov discovered antigravity.

or jump to the opposite shortcut:

The claim is false.

An inquiry-oriented architecture should resist both shortcuts when the available semantic field does not justify them.

Its strength is not that it produces a stronger opinion. Its strength is that it preserves the difference between:

known
claimed
supported
contradicted
uncertain
unknown

19. COSMOS, HOLOFLUX, and IOP

HOLOFLUX
Meaning + Explication

IOP
Intent + Understanding

COSMOS
Orchestration of the Whole

Together:

20. Toward an executable COSMOS DSL

cosmos :research_system do
  intent :understand

  context do
    source :primary_document
  end

  policies do
    preserve :provenance
    preserve :unknown
    preserve :contradiction
  end

  capabilities do
    use :retrieval
    use :holoflux
    use :iop
  end

  orchestrate do
    integrate :understanding
  end

  project do
    as :article
    as :diagram
    as :agent_behavior
  end
end

The DSL would no longer merely describe a workflow. It would describe what kind of cognitive system should exist. The runtime would determine how to instantiate it.

21. The larger shift

Software abstractions have repeatedly moved upward:

Machine Instructions
       ↓
Procedural Programming
       ↓
Object-Oriented Programming
       ↓
Distributed Systems
       ↓
Cloud-Native Systems
       ↓
Agentic Systems

AI-native software may require another set of first-class concepts:

Intent
Meaning
Context
Evidence
Uncertainty
Inquiry
Understanding

Perhaps the important transition is not merely:

software → agents

but:

execution → inquiry

and eventually:

opaque reasoning → explicit understanding

Conclusion

AI agents already know how to act. Increasingly, they know how to choose tools, delegate work, maintain context, inspect results, and continue autonomously.

The next architectural question may be different.

Can an AI-native system make explicit:

what was observed
what was claimed
where it came from
what supports it
what contradicts it
what remains uncertain
what remains unknown
what can actually be understood

If so, the fundamental loop changes:

becomes:

The system no longer asks only:

What should I do next?

It can also ask:

What is actually happening?

What do I know?

What don’t I know?

And what do I truly understand?

That is where HOLOFLUX, IOP, and COSMOS begin to converge — not merely into another agent framework, but into an architecture for AI-native understanding.

Core formulas

HOLOFLUX = Meaning + Explication
IOP = Intent + Understanding
COSMOS = Orchestration of the Whole

References

  • Grebennikov, Viktor S. — My World, Chapter 5. English translation of “The Natural Phenomena of AntiGravitation and Invisibility in Insects due to the Grebennikov Cavity Structure Effect (CSE).” Used here as a primary source for Grebennikov’s claims, not as independent confirmation. https://geomagnetics.org/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/myworldbyviktorgrebennikovfinpdf.pdf
  • OpenAI — Agents documentation. Contemporary reference for agent loops, tools, handoffs, guardrails, state, and orchestration. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents
  • David Bohm. The implicate/explicate order is used here as a conceptual analogy, not as a claim that HOLOFLUX implements Bohm’s physical theory. https://www.davidbohm.net/
  • J. Krishnamurti. Observation, conditioning, attention, conflict, ending, and insight inform the inquiry vocabulary used here as conceptual inspiration rather than deterministic formalization. https://www.jkrishnamurti.org/

Related concepts

  • HOLOFLUX — Meaning + Explication
  • IOP — Intent + Understanding
  • COSMOS — Intent-driven orchestration of knowledge, meaning, intelligence, and creation
  • IMPLICATE — Enfolded semantic order from which explicit representations can emerge
  • FACTORIES — Engines of explication that transform structured meaning and intent into explicit, communicable digital media

entry.title: From Ericsson Use Cases to AI-Native Systems

link.title: From Ericsson Use Cases to AI-Native Systems

entry.content:
The use case is the boundary that transforms human intention into a distributed AI architecture.

Contents

  • The AI-Native question
  • Ivar Jacobson and Ericsson
  • AXE, PLEX and Function Blocks
  • HLPLEX, processes and FORLOPP
  • From Ericsson languages to concurrent systems
  • From function blocks to AI building blocks
  • One use case, decomposed end to end
  • The use case as an AI boundary
  • When context becomes a layer above the function
  • Conclusion

The AI-Native question

The AI industry often presents intention-driven systems as something entirely new. But an AI-Native system does not simply receive an intention and autonomously invent the entire solution.

It must understand what the intention means, determine what the system is responsible for, identify the participating actors, decompose the business process and select the appropriate capabilities.

The real starting point is not the agent.

It is the use case.

Actor
  → Intent
    → Use Case
      → Business Process
        → Responsibilities
          → AI Building Blocks
            → Outcome

The use case turns an intention into a bounded responsibility. It tells the system who participates, what must happen, what is allowed, what is outside the boundary, what counts as success and what evidence must be produced.

A requirement states what should happen. A use case defines the bounded process through which it can happen.

Ivar Jacobson and Ericsson

Before use cases became widely associated with UML, Objectory and the Rational Unified Process, Ivar Jacobson was working at Ericsson on large, real-time telecom systems such as AKE and AXE, including PLEX.

Jacobson is widely credited with introducing use cases in 1986 as a way to specify functional software requirements. The idea emerged from a practical problem: how to understand systems whose behaviour was distributed across software units, processes, signals and hardware.

The historical connection matters because the use case was not created as a decorative documentation technique. It was a way to reason about responsibility:

Who interacts with the system?
What does the actor need to accomplish?
What functions are required?
Where does each responsibility live?
How do the units cooperate?

AXE, PLEX and Function Blocks

The AXE system gives this history a concrete form. PLEX-C was used to produce software for the central processor of the AXE control system. Functional blocks could also involve hardware and regional software running in regional processors.

This meant that a system function was not necessarily located in one place:

Central Software
  + Regional Software
    + Hardware
      + Functional Blocks
        + Signals

The conceptual decomposition was:

Actor
  → Use Case
    → System Function
      → Function Block
        → Software Unit
          → Process
            → Signal / Event

A Function Block was not simply a source-code file. It represented a function within a larger application system, potentially combining software, local data, signal interfaces, associated hardware and regional software.

Legend: the Function Block is the unit of composition within the application system; it brings together software, data, interfaces and physical or regional resources.

The use case gave the function its reason for existing. The Function Block gave the function an architectural home.

HLPLEX, processes and FORLOPP

HLPLEX made active execution and concurrency more explicit. Modules could contain processes; processes could execute concurrently, have multiple instances and communicate through event paths.

Function Block
  └── Module
       ├── Process A
       ├── Process B
       └── Process C

Process A
  → Event
    → Process B

The unit was no longer only a container of functionality. It became an active participant in a larger process.

The AXE documentation also describes FORLOPP as a sequence of events. When multiple Function Blocks participated in the same call, records could be linked into a chain with a Forlopp Identity, or FID.

Call
  → Record in Block A
    → Record in Block B
      → Record in Block C
        → Record in Block D

FID = identity of the distributed call

The FID allowed the system to identify and release a specific call in the event of a software failure. This is not identical to a modern trace ID or agent run ID, but the architectural question is related:

How does one preserve the identity of an operation while it crosses multiple units?

From Ericsson languages to concurrent systems

The historical arc can be read as:

PLEX
  → HLPLEX
    → Erlang
      → Elixir

This should not be understood as a direct succession of compilers or language versions. PLEX and HLPLEX were Ericsson languages and execution environments for telecom systems; Erlang emerged later from the same Ericsson context and addressed related problems at a broader level.

The important continuity is architectural:

PLEX / HLPLEX
  → Function Blocks
  → Processes
  → Events and Signals
  → Distributed Execution

Erlang / Elixir
  → Processes
  → Message Passing
  → Isolation
  → Supervision
  → Fault Tolerance

Erlang and Elixir therefore belong to a longer Ericsson tradition of decomposing complex systems into interacting, concurrent and recoverable units. The lineage is not only syntactic. It is a lineage of architectural concerns: decomposition, communication, concurrency, isolation, supervision and composition.

AI-Native systems extend this lineage with another layer:

Distributed Execution
  → Intent
    → Context
      → Adaptive Feedback

The function is still distributed, but its participation can now be directed by an intention and the context in which that intention is being pursued.

From function blocks to AI building blocks

The history of software paradigms is also a history of changing answers to one question:

What is the right unit for realizing a responsibility?

OOP
  → Object = data + behaviour

PLEX
  → Function Block = function + software + hardware

HLPLEX
  → Process = state + behaviour + events

Erlang / Elixir
  → Process = isolation + messages + supervision

Ruby / Ractors
  → Unit = isolation + parallel execution

AI-Native
  → Agent = state + behaviour + intent + feedback

The paradigms are not identical and do not form a simple chain of direct inheritance. They respond to related pressures: decomposition, encapsulation, communication, concurrency, recovery, composition and responsibility.

An AI-Native system is not composed only of agents. It is composed of different building blocks, each with a distinct role:

Responsibility Building block
Specialized knowledge Skill / RAG
Concrete execution Tool
External integration MCP
Known sequence Workflow
Adaptive judgment Agent
Persistent context Memory
Lifecycle control Hook
Sensitive authorization Human actor

The use case determines which of these are necessary.

One use case, decomposed end to end

Consider this intention:

Investigate a production incident and produce a verified report.

Before decomposing this intention into AI building blocks, we can express it as a classic use case: an authorized engineer interacts with an incident-investigation system to obtain a verified report and, when necessary, approve a risky change.

Legend: the use case diagram identifies the actor, the system boundary, the goal and the controlled extension requiring authorization.

This is not yet an architecture. We first turn it into a bounded use case:

An authorized engineer requests an investigation. The system gathers relevant documentation and telemetry, forms and tests hypotheses, records evidence, produces a report and requests human approval before any risky production change.

The use case diagram defines the goal and the system boundary. The sequence below shows how that goal is realized over time, with context directing which capabilities participate at each stage.

Legend: the sequence shows context as an active participant in execution, not merely as information loaded before the agent starts.

The distributed business process becomes visible:

Incident Investigation
  ├── receive the request
  ├── identify the affected service
  ├── retrieve relevant documentation
  ├── inspect logs and metrics
  ├── form hypotheses
  ├── run safe verification steps
  ├── evaluate evidence
  ├── produce a report
  └── request approval for risky action

Each responsibility can now be assigned to an appropriate participant:

Receive and classify request       → Coordinator Agent
Retrieve runbooks and documentation → RAG
Apply incident procedure           → Skill
Query logs and metrics             → Tool
Connect to observability systems   → MCP
Compare hypotheses                 → Investigation Agent
Execute standard checks            → Workflow
Preserve findings and context      → Memory
Block unsafe operations            → Hook / Policy
Approve production changes         → Human Actor

Legend: the diagram separates context, execution and governance; the use case routes the intention through bounded capabilities toward evidence and human-verified completion.

The diagram does not show one super-agent performing everything. It shows a distributed process in which each building block has a bounded responsibility.

The use case as an AI boundary

The use case is the boundary that transforms intention into AI architecture:

Use Case
  → defines purpose
    → assigns responsibility
      → restricts authority
        → selects building blocks
          → defines completion

For every agent, skill, tool or workflow, we should be able to ask:

Which use case requires this?
Which responsibility does it realize?
What authority does it have?
What does it communicate?
What evidence does it produce?
When must it stop?

This prevents common category errors:

Agent ≠ Skill
Skill ≠ Tool
Tool ≠ MCP
MCP ≠ RAG
RAG ≠ Memory
Hook ≠ Workflow

Not every responsibility needs to become an agent. Not every capability needs autonomy. Not every document needs to become memory. Not every integration needs to become an MCP server.

The use case must decide.

Intention should not be confused with a prompt. A prompt is one possible interface to an AI model; an intention is the human or business purpose that gives the system direction.

Intention ≠ Prompt
Intention → Use Case → Context → AI Execution

The use case also defines what must not happen: actions outside the scope, capabilities without authority, data that cannot be used, decisions that require human approval and conditions under which execution must stop. This negative space is part of the architecture.

When context becomes a layer above the function

In a traditional distributed system, the main architectural question was often where a function should execute:

Use Case
  → System Function
    → Function Block
      → Process
        → Signal

In an AI-Native system, the functions still exist, but a contextual layer helps decide which ones should participate in the current situation:

Intent
  → Use Case
    → Context
      → Responsibilities
        → Functions and AI Building Blocks
          → Action and Evidence

Consider the same production incident under two different contexts:

Context Directed execution
A service is degraded, but no data loss is detected Retrieve runbooks, inspect metrics and perform safe diagnostics
The same service shows possible data corruption Retrieve recovery procedures, increase evidence requirements and require human approval before changes

The underlying functions may be similar, but the context changes their order, authority and level of caution. In the first situation, a diagnostic workflow may be enough. In the second, the system may need additional RAG sources, a specialized skill, an investigation agent, stronger hooks and a human checkpoint.

This is the additional layer introduced by AI-Native systems:

Function = what can be done
Context  = what matters now
Use Case = why it is being done and where it must stop

The use case therefore does not replace the distributed function. It gives direction to the function through context, throughout execution.

In this sense, intention becomes an architectural input:

Intent
  → Use Case
    → Context
      → System Boundary
        → Responsibilities
          → AI Building Blocks

The use case is the bridge between human intention and system design. It turns intention into a bounded context in which AI can reason, act, produce evidence and stop.

Conclusion

The history of software composition can be read as a history of changing units:

Object
  → Function Block
    → Process
      → Supervised Application
        → Ractor
          → Agent

Each unit addressed a different aspect of complexity:

Object           → encapsulation
Function Block   → functional composition
Process          → active execution
Message          → communication
Supervision      → recovery
Ractor           → isolation and parallelism
Agent            → intention and adaptive action

But the unit alone is never enough. A system also needs purpose, responsibility, authority, context, constraints, evidence and completion.

The use case provides that definition. It is where a human intention becomes a system responsibility, where a business process becomes an architectural boundary and where the system decides what belongs inside the solution and what must remain outside it.

AI-Native systems do not begin with agents. They begin with intentions that become use cases, use cases that become responsibilities, and responsibilities that become carefully chosen building blocks.

The use case is where intention becomes architecture. It does not remove the need for system modeling; it gives system modeling a more direct starting point.

References

  • Ivar Jacobson — biography and work
  • Ivar Jacobson International
  • Object Management Group — UML
  • Ruby Ractor documentation
  • Model Context Protocol
  • Google Cloud — Agentic AI security operations workflow

The AXE, PLEX and HLPLEX historical details in this article were checked against Ericsson training manuals supplied as research material. The article paraphrases those materials and does not reproduce their proprietary diagrams or code.

entry.title: From the Architecture of the Mind to AI-Native Intelligence

link.title: From the Architecture of the Mind to AI-Native Intelligence

entry.content:
Modern AI borrowed the vocabulary of the mind. The more interesting question is whether it also preserved the distinctions behind that vocabulary.

Contents

  1. AI already speaks the language of the mind
  2. Memory is not knowledge
  3. Attention is not necessarily attention
  4. Observation is not interpretation
  5. Retrieval is not evidence
  6. Current AI-native architecture is largely operational
  7. From an operational loop to an epistemic loop
  8. The unknown should be a valid computational state
  9. Contradiction should not merely be suppressed
  10. From Ruby metaphor to an experimental cognitive DSL
  11. A DSL can become a semantic model
  12. Three layers of AI-native architecture
  13. Memory, knowledge, and understanding
  14. Reasoning may not be enough
  15. From answer generation to inquiry
  16. Returning to Krishnamurti
  17. Architecture of Inquiry
  18. Conceptual notes
  19. References

In Architecture of the Mind, we used systems thinking, software architecture, and Ruby as metaphors for exploring some of J. Krishnamurti’s observations about conditioning, memory, knowledge, thought, attention, insight, and action.

The architecture revolved around a simple question:

Can the brain meet what-is directly, without translating the present through the accumulated past?

The model deliberately distinguished two movements.

The first was the recursive movement of the known:

The second pointed toward something very different:

The architecture was never intended to claim that the human mind is software.

It was a map.

And as the previous post emphasized:

The description is not the described.

That distinction becomes even more important when we turn toward artificial intelligence.

Modern AI already speaks extensively in the vocabulary of cognition: memory, attention, reasoning, knowledge, reflection, planning, learning, intelligence, agents.

But borrowing the vocabulary of the mind does not necessarily mean that we have preserved the distinctions behind it.

This raises a different question:

What happens if we use the architecture of the mind not as a blueprint for AI, but as a way of questioning AI architecture?

That takes us from an Architecture of the Mind toward an Architecture of AI-Native Intelligence.

1. AI already speaks the language of the mind

Modern AI systems increasingly operate through loops rather than isolated model calls.

An agent can receive a goal, interpret instructions, maintain context, call tools, inspect results, transfer work to another agent, preserve state, and continue until a stopping condition is reached.

At a high level, we could simplify much of today’s agentic architecture as:

This is already substantially different from conventional application architecture.

Traditional software commonly defines the path in advance:

INPUT → FUNCTION → FUNCTION → FUNCTION → OUTPUT

Agentic software increasingly describes:

goal
context
capabilities
constraints
environment

and allows the model and runtime to determine part of the path.

That is an important characteristic of AI-native systems.

But something remains hidden inside the loop.

What does the system actually understand while it is doing this?

2. Memory is not knowledge

One of the distinctions from the earlier architecture immediately becomes useful.

There, memory and knowledge participated in the same movement but were not identical:

EXPERIENCE → MEMORY → KNOWLEDGE → THOUGHT

The distinction becomes equally useful in AI.

An AI system may contain:

context window
conversation history
retrieved documents
vector embeddings
persistent state
event history
model parameters
external databases

We often group several of these under the word memory.

But they perform different functions.

A conversation history is not the same thing as a retrieved document. A retrieved document is not the same thing as model parameters. Persisted workflow state is not necessarily knowledge. And none of them automatically constitutes understanding.

CONVERSATION HISTORY
        ≠
RETRIEVED INFORMATION
        ≠
MODEL KNOWLEDGE
        ≠
WORKFLOW STATE
        ≠
UNDERSTANDING

When information becomes available to an AI system, has the system remembered something, known something, or understood something?

Those are not necessarily the same event.

3. Attention is not necessarily attention

The word attention provides an even clearer example.

In machine learning, attention refers to computational mechanisms that weight relationships among representations.

In Krishnamurti’s vocabulary, attention points toward something very different.

The previous architecture described choiceless awareness as observation without a psychological controller continuously deciding:

keep this
reject that
believe this
avoid that

These concepts should not be collapsed.

We should not write:

Transformer attention = Krishnamurti's attention

A more careful relationship is:

HUMAN / PHILOSOPHICAL CONCEPT
            ↓
     FUNCTIONAL ANALOGY
            ↓
COMPUTATIONAL IMPLEMENTATION

For example:

ATTENTION

Krishnamurti:
observation without psychological choice

AI systems:
representation weighting
context selection
retrieval
routing
salience

There may be useful functional parallels.

There is no reason to assume conceptual identity.

And the mismatch itself may be more interesting than the similarity.

4. Observation is not interpretation

The distinction between observation and interpretation may be even more important for AI architecture.

The earlier model began with:

WHAT-IS → OBSERVATION

But it also showed another movement:

WHAT-IS → MEMORY → KNOWLEDGE → THOUGHT → INTERPRETATION

The same distinction appears constantly in AI systems.

Suppose an agent reads a deployment log containing:

The application stopped responding at 14:03 UTC.

That statement comes from an external source.

The model may then generate:

The deployment probably failed because
the database migration timed out.

These are epistemically different objects.

The first is closer to source / observation. The second is interpretation / claim.

Yet generated answers can easily flatten them into a single paragraph.

A more explicit architecture would preserve the movement:

and then ask:

What evidence supports the claim?

This changes the role of the architecture.

It is no longer concerned only with execution.

It begins to represent how the system came to hold something as meaningful or plausible.

5. Retrieval is not evidence

This distinction exposes another common shortcut.

An AI system retrieves a document.

Therefore it has a source.

But:

SOURCE ≠ EVIDENCE

A source may contain evidence. It may also contain opinion, speculation, incorrect information, conflicting interpretation, historical information that no longer applies, or statements irrelevant to the claim being evaluated.

So a more careful architecture might require:

SOURCE → PASSAGE → OBSERVATION → EVIDENCE → CLAIM

rather than:

SOURCE → ANSWER

Access to more information does not automatically produce better understanding.

Sometimes it merely produces more material to interpret.

6. Current AI-native architecture is largely operational

If we simplify today’s agent systems, their strongest abstractions tend to surround execution.

GOAL → PLAN → TOOL → RESULT → STATE → NEXT ACTION

Supporting concepts include:

instructions
models
tools
MCP
handoffs
guardrails
sandboxing
state
memory
tracing
evaluation

These are powerful capabilities.

They are increasingly sophisticated at answering:

What should happen next?

But consider a different set of questions:

What was actually observed?
What was inferred?
What is merely assumed?
What is being claimed?
What supports that claim?
What contradicts it?
What remains unknown?
What changed the current understanding?

These concepts can certainly be implemented today.

But they are not necessarily first-class semantic elements of the underlying agent runtime.

That suggests another architectural layer.

From implementation structure toward engineering meaning: intent, context, evidence, verification, observation, and feedback become architectural concerns.

7. From an operational loop to an epistemic loop

The conventional agent loop asks something like:

What should I do next to complete this goal?

Imagine adding another question:

What do I currently understand, and why?

The architecture changes.

Instead of primarily:

PLAN → EXECUTE → OBSERVE RESULT → PLAN AGAIN

we begin to see:

Action remains important.

But action now emerges from an evolving epistemic state.

This is no longer merely an agent completing a task.

It is a system whose state of understanding changes through interaction.

The operational loop asks what to do next. The epistemic loop asks what is currently understood, what supports it, and what remains unresolved.

8. The unknown should be a valid computational state

Software engineering often prefers explicit states:

true / false
success / failure
valid / invalid
completed / pending

Generative AI introduced probability and ambiguity into software execution, but applications still frequently push models toward producing an answer.

An architecture of inquiry should allow another state:

UNKNOWN

Not error. Not nil. Not failure.

But:

There is currently insufficient basis for understanding this.

Consider:

inquiry "Why did the deployment fail?" do
  observe "Service became unavailable at 14:03 UTC"

  claim "The database migration caused the failure" do
    confidence :low
  end

  evidence "deployment.log" do
    supports :partial
  end

  conclude :unknown
end

The system has still learned something.

It knows what was observed, what is suspected, what evidence exists, and what remains missing.

UNKNOWN ≠ NOTHING

An explicit unknown may contain considerable structure.

Perhaps an intelligent system should sometimes become more precise about what it does not know, rather than more confident about an answer.

9. Contradiction should not merely be suppressed

Suppose two sources support incompatible claims.

A system optimized primarily for answer generation may attempt to synthesize them immediately.

But contradiction itself can be useful information.

SOURCE A → CLAIM X
SOURCE B → CLAIM NOT-X

Instead of forcing X or NOT-X, an epistemic architecture could represent:

CONTRADICTION

and preserve claim A, claim B, source A, source B, context, confidence, and time.

The contradiction then becomes a trigger for inquiry:

CONTRADICTION → NEW QUESTION → NEW EVIDENCE → REVISION

The architecture is not trying to eliminate ambiguity as quickly as possible.

It is trying to understand why the ambiguity exists.

10. From Ruby metaphor to an experimental cognitive DSL

The previous post used Ruby to make the architecture of mind easier to see.

We can now take the metaphor one step further.

Suppose we describe an architecture not primarily in terms of objects and services, but in terms of epistemic distinctions.

architecture :intelligence do
  distinguish :observation, :interpretation
  distinguish :memory, :knowledge, :understanding
  distinguish :source, :evidence, :claim

  preserve :unknown
  expose :uncertainty
  detect :contradiction

  inquiry do
    observe
    question
    hypothesize
    seek_evidence
    revise
  end

  act only_from: :current_understanding
end

This is still Ruby-like syntax.

But notice what it describes.

Not merely what the machine should execute, but how the system should relate observation, interpretation, evidence, uncertainty, and understanding.

We could make it concrete:

inquiry "What caused the outage?" do
  observe "Health checks started failing at 14:03"

  distinguish do
    fact       "Health checks failed"
    hypothesis "Database saturation caused the outage"
    assumption "Traffic increased immediately beforehand"
  end

  claim "Database saturation caused the outage" do
    confidence :medium
  end

  require_evidence do
    database_metrics
    request_traces
    deployment_history
  end

  preserve_unknown unless: :sufficient_evidence
end

The architecture now exposes distinctions that are usually buried inside a prompt or a generated response.

That alone may be useful.

11. A DSL can become a semantic model

Once these elements are explicit, the DSL does not need to remain text.

It can become an intermediate semantic representation.

The diagram is no longer merely an illustration manually drawn after the architecture was designed.

It becomes a projection of the architecture itself.

This introduces an interesting possibility:

Code, diagrams, explanations, traces, and runtime state could be different views of the same semantic structure.

12. Three layers of AI-native architecture

This suggests separating AI-native architecture into at least three conceptual layers.

The intent layer expresses why something is being attempted.

The operational layer provides the capabilities needed to perform the work.

Modern agent frameworks are increasingly sophisticated in this operational layer: tools, MCP, handoffs, state, sandbox environments, guardrails, tracing, and multi-agent orchestration are becoming standard architectural concerns.

The proposed epistemic layer asks different questions:

What was observed?
What is being inferred?
What is merely assumed?
What is the claim?
Where did the supporting information originate?
What counts as evidence?
What contradicts the current model?
What remains uncertain?
What is currently understood?

This layer does not replace agent orchestration.

It complements it.

An AI-native system can be viewed as more than operational orchestration: intent, epistemic state, and execution form distinct but connected layers.

13. Memory, knowledge, and understanding

We can now return to perhaps the most important distinction:

MEMORY ≠ KNOWLEDGE ≠ UNDERSTANDING

A possible computational interpretation is:

Memory

What has been retained?

Knowledge

What information is currently available?

Understanding

What relationships does the system
currently hold as meaningful,
and on what basis?

Understanding would therefore involve more than stored information.

It may require relationships among:

Claims
Evidence
Sources
Context
Perspective
Contradictions
Uncertainty
Time
Provenance

Most importantly, understanding would need to be revisable.

UNDERSTANDING(t0)
        ↓
NEW OBSERVATION
        ↓
CONTRADICTION
        ↓
INQUIRY
        ↓
UNDERSTANDING(t1)

Understanding becomes less like a stored answer and more like a living semantic state.

14. Reasoning may not be enough

Reasoning is already central to contemporary AI.

Models can decompose problems, select tools, evaluate intermediate results, revise plans, and perform increasingly long sequences of work.

But an important distinction emerges:

REASONING ≠ UNDERSTANDING

Reasoning describes a process.

Understanding describes a state of meaningful relationships produced or revised through that process.

A system can reason from a false assumption. It can produce a coherent derivation from unreliable evidence. It can plan effectively toward a misunderstood objective.

So an architecture of intelligence may need to ask not only:

Can the model reason?

but:

What is the reasoning operating on?
Which observations are trusted?
Which assumptions were introduced?
Which evidence supports the conclusion?
What remains unresolved?

Reasoning becomes one part of inquiry rather than the whole architecture.

15. From answer generation to inquiry

This may reveal a deeper transition.

Much of generative AI began with:

PROMPT → MODEL → ANSWER

Agentic AI extended this toward:

GOAL → PLAN → TOOLS → ACTION → RESULT

An architecture of inquiry would add another movement:

INTENT
  ↓
OBSERVATION
  ↓
QUESTION
  ↓
INTERPRETATION
  ↓
CLAIM
  ↓
EVIDENCE
  ↓
UNCERTAINTY
  ↓
UNDERSTANDING
  ↓
ACTION

and then:

ACTION → NEW OBSERVATION → REVISED UNDERSTANDING

This makes the architecture recursive.

But unlike a simple execution loop, what changes after each iteration is not merely the plan.

What changes is the system’s semantic relationship to the problem.

16. Returning to Krishnamurti

At this point, it is important to return to where the investigation began.

Krishnamurti’s exploration of memory, thought, attention, insight, and intelligence should not be translated mechanically into software architecture.

We should resist equations such as:

human memory = vector database
thought = token generation
attention = attention matrix
insight = inference
intelligence = model capability

The value of the comparison lies in doing the opposite:

preserving the distinctions.

The previous architecture asked:

Can the brain meet what-is directly, without translating the present through the accumulated past?

For AI architecture, a related question might be:

Can an intelligent system distinguish what it observes from what it generates about what it observes?

Then another:

Can it distinguish information from interpretation, evidence from claim, and accumulated knowledge from current understanding?

And perhaps another:

Can it remain with the unknown when the available evidence does not justify a conclusion?

These may be more interesting architectural questions than simply asking how many tools an agent can invoke.

17. Architecture of Inquiry

Modern AI borrowed much of the vocabulary of the mind.

Memory
Attention
Reasoning
Learning
Knowledge
Intelligence
Agents

But vocabulary can hide differences.

A word that sounds familiar may represent a completely different mechanism.

The interesting task, therefore, is not to claim that AI reproduces the mind.

It is to use these conceptual differences to ask better architectural questions.

Perhaps an AI-native architecture should explicitly represent:

what was observed
what was retrieved
what was interpreted
what was assumed
what is being claimed
what evidence supports it
what contradicts it
what remains unknown
what changed
what is currently understood

This would shift part of the emphasis from answer generation toward inquiry.

From:

GOAL → PLAN → EXECUTE

Toward:

The system still needs models.

It still needs memory.

It still needs tools.

It still needs planning, execution, state, guardrails, and observability.

But perhaps these are not the entire architecture of intelligence.

Perhaps AI-native systems should represent not only what they can do, but also:

what they know, what they assume, what they cannot yet establish, and how their understanding changes.

That would take us beyond an architecture of agents.

It would begin to look like an:

Architecture of Inquiry

And perhaps that is where the next investigation should begin.

Conceptual notes

This post continues the systems-thinking approach introduced in Architecture of the Mind: A Visual Model Through Ruby and Systems Thinking, where memory, knowledge, thought, conditioning, awareness, insight, and action were represented as related movements rather than isolated components.

The comparison with current AI architecture is deliberately functional, not ontological. Computational memory is not human memory; machine-learning attention is not choiceless attention; model inference is not thought in Krishnamurti’s sense; and no claim is made here that current AI systems possess consciousness or human understanding.

The purpose of the comparison is narrower:

to discover whether distinctions developed while investigating the mind can help us design more explicit, inspectable, and epistemically disciplined AI systems.

link.title: Beyond the Sphinx — Architecture for Deep Time

entry.content:
To researchers, archaeologists, and independent thinkers who keep exploring Egypt with rigor and imagination — reminding us that the past is not a closed book, but a deeper conversation with time.

Perhaps the mystery is not what Egypt wanted to tell us, but why it built as if time itself were part of the audience.

Some monuments are made for a generation.

Others are made for a dynasty.

And then there are structures whose scale, material and mass seem to belong to a different category altogether: architecture that can survive the disappearance of the people who built it.

The pyramids of Giza are still here after roughly four and a half millennia. The Osireion at Abydos still holds its monumental stone architecture below ground. At Hawara, little remains above the surface of the temple complex that ancient authors called the Labyrinth, yet archaeology and geophysics continue to recover traces of what once stood there.

This article begins where The Secret of the Sphinx ended.

That earlier journey asked whether the Sphinx and pyramids could be read symbolically as a compass carried across civilizational cycles.

Here the question is different.

Why build for deep time at all?

And if Egypt’s monumental architecture was deliberately made to endure, what are we still failing to understand about it?

At a Glance

This article follows five layers:

  1. What is confirmed — spaces and structures established through archaeology or reproducible measurement.
  2. What remains unknown — features whose purpose or full extent is still unresolved.
  3. What is claimed — recent interpretations that have not yet received independent archaeological confirmation.
  4. What is remembered — ancient descriptions such as the Labyrinth at Hawara and Egypt’s own language of primordial order.
  5. What the architecture suggests philosophically — not a hidden message asserted as fact, but a question about permanence, memory and time.

The distinction matters.

A mystery becomes more interesting, not less, when we know exactly where the evidence ends.

Evidence Key

🟢 Confirmed — supported by archaeology, direct observation or reproducible measurement.
🟡 Historical — preserved in ancient texts, excavation records or documented tradition, but not necessarily fully reconstructed.
🟣 Interpretive — a symbolic, ritual or initiatory reading that goes beyond what archaeology alone can establish.
🔵 Esoteric / visionary — material from psychic, occult or revelatory traditions, presented as such rather than as archaeological evidence.

The same monument may appear in more than one layer. The label tells us what kind of claim is being made, not whether the subject is worth exploring.

Contents

  • From Legacy to Permanence
  • Architecture for Deep Time
  • The Pyramid Is Still Not Fully Known
  • Beneath Giza: Signal Is Not Structure
  • The Osireion: Architecture Below Time
  • Hawara and the Memory of the Labyrinth
  • The Initiatory Geography Hypothesis
  • Edgar Cayce and the Hall of Records
  • Before Egypt Was Egypt
  • Atlantis: Answer or Archetype?
  • Built to Cross Ages
  • Time as the Audience
  • What Have We Not Yet Learned to Read?
  • As Before, So After
  • References and Further Reading

From Legacy to Permanence

The previous article explored the possibility of a legacy intended for future humanity.

This time we do not begin with the message.

We begin with the medium.

Stone.

Not a tablet that can be carried away. Not a manuscript dependent on language. Not an institution dependent on political continuity.

A mountain of engineered stone.

That changes the question.

Why choose a medium whose useful lifetime exceeds the civilization that produced it?

The conventional archaeological answers remain essential. Egyptian monumental architecture expressed royal power, funerary belief, cult, cosmic order and the transformation of the king. None of that needs to be discarded.

But permanence itself deserves attention.

A monument may communicate through inscriptions.

A megalithic monument also communicates through its continued existence.

Architecture for Deep Time

“Deep time” is normally a geological idea: a scale so large that an individual human life becomes almost negligible.

Megalithic architecture creates something analogous in culture.

A person dies.

A dynasty ends.

A language changes.

A religion transforms.

The stone remains.

This does not prove that the builders intended to address people thousands of years in the future.

But it establishes something simpler and observable:

the architecture was capable of doing so.

That capacity becomes part of the monument’s historical afterlife.

The Pyramid Is Still Not Fully Known

The Great Pyramid is one of the most studied buildings on Earth.

It still surprises us.

In 2017, the ScanPyramids collaboration reported the detection of a previously unknown large void above the Grand Gallery using cosmic-ray muography. The signal was independently observed with three detector systems. The feature, known as the ScanPyramids Big Void, has a minimum length of about 30 metres. Its purpose remains unknown.

That distinction is crucial:

existence: strongly supported.

function: unknown.

In 2023 a corridor behind the chevron-shaped stones on the north face of the pyramid was directly imaged. In 2025, researchers published a multimodal confirmation using ground-penetrating radar, ultrasonic testing and electrical resistivity tomography.

Four and a half millennia after construction, the architectural map is still being refined.

That fact alone should make us cautious about statements beginning with “we already know exactly what the pyramid is.”

The important point is not that a dramatic secret must exist.

It is almost the opposite.

The unknown can be real without our interpretation of it being correct.

Beneath Giza: Signal Is Not Structure

In 2025, dramatic claims spread internationally about enormous structures supposedly detected hundreds of metres beneath the Pyramid of Khafre using a satellite-based interpretation of synthetic aperture radar data.

The published visualizations were extraordinary: deep shafts, cylindrical forms and enormous geometric structures beneath the plateau.

They were also not an archaeological discovery in the established sense.

Radar specialists and Egyptologists challenged the physical ability of the method to resolve structures at the claimed depths, and no excavation or independent geophysical survey has confirmed the proposed underground architecture.

By 2026 the claim remained unverified.

This makes it useful for the article — not as evidence of a lost city, but as a demonstration of how easily a signal can become a story.

This sequence should become one of our rules for the entire investigation:

Signal is not structure. Structure is not date. Date is not meaning.

The temptation is to jump from the first box to the last.

Archaeology exists precisely because we should not.

The Osireion: Architecture Below Time

If Giza confronts us with spaces we are still discovering, Abydos confronts us with something different.

The Osireion, behind the Temple of Seti I, is monumental, subterranean and visually austere. Massive granite elements surround a central architectural core associated with water. Its style feels radically different from the richly decorated temple nearby.

That difference has encouraged modern claims that the structure might be vastly older than Seti I.

The archaeological record does not currently support that conclusion.

Early excavators were themselves struck by the structure. Later work by Henri Frankfort connected the monument structurally and epigraphically with Seti I’s complex. The Egypt Exploration Society describes the Osireion as the enigmatic structure behind Seti’s temple, and the standard interpretation treats it as a cenotaph or symbolic tomb associated with Osiris and the royal funerary program.

The interesting question therefore is not:

Was the Osireion built by Atlantis?

There is no archaeological basis for stating that.

The better question is:

Why did New Kingdom Egyptians deliberately build a structure that evokes an architecture of primordial permanence?

Its subterranean character matters.

Its water symbolism matters.

Its monumental stonework matters.

And Abydos itself matters: by the Middle Kingdom it had become Egypt’s principal cult centre for Osiris.

The structure appears almost designed to make the visitor descend out of ordinary historical time.

Osiris and Reconstruction

There is a philosophical correspondence here worth making explicit — as interpretation, not archaeology.

Osiris is dismembered.

The fragments are gathered.

Order is reconstructed.

Something returns in another form.

The same pattern describes our relationship with ancient civilizations.

The monument survives.

Meaning fragments.

Every later civilization tries to assemble it again.

Hawara and the Memory of the Labyrinth

At Hawara, south of the pyramid of Amenemhat III, the situation is almost reversed.

Instead of an enormous monument surviving nearly intact, we have the memory of something extraordinary whose visible architecture was largely destroyed.

Ancient Greek authors described an Egyptian Labyrinth of remarkable scale. Modern archaeology identifies the principal mortuary temple of Amenemhat III at Hawara with that tradition. Petrie excavated the site in the nineteenth century, but found that much of the monumental complex had already been destroyed and quarried.

Yet the site did not become archaeologically empty.

A 2000 survey recovered additional evidence associated with the temple complex. A peer-reviewed 2010 geophysical study reported shallow elongated and square anomalies whose spatial distribution significantly matched aspects of the historical description.

A 2025 paper went further, interpreting satellite SAR imagery as possible evidence for a much larger buried structure.

That latest interpretation should be treated cautiously. Space-based radar claims about deeply buried architecture require independent validation, especially after the controversy surrounding similar claims at Giza.

But Hawara differs from the Khafre story in one important respect:

the Labyrinth is not invented by the modern scan.

Its historical and archaeological existence as Amenemhat III’s temple complex is already well established.

The open questions concern its original form, extent, surviving subsurface remains and how much of the ancient descriptions should be read literally.

The Initiatory Geography Hypothesis

Herodotus places the Labyrinth near Lake Moeris, in the Fayum region, not beneath Giza. The historical Labyrinth and the controversial structures recently claimed beneath the Giza plateau are therefore not the same archaeological claim.

Yet a later initiatory interpretation makes a different connection. In La pirámide iniciática, Joan Llarch asks whether a triple subterranean path could begin at the Sphinx, lead toward the three pyramids and continue toward the Labyrinth described by Herodotus.

This hypothesis directly echoes the reading developed in The Secret of the Sphinx, where the Sphinx is approached as a threshold to an initiatory journey through the Giza complex. Here, however, the question is widened: could that initiatory geography be not only symbolic and ritual, but also reflect a physical organization of space that is now only partially known?

This is not established archaeology, and it should not be presented as a geographical reading of Herodotus. It is better understood as an initiatory geography: the possibility that the Sphinx, the pyramids and the Labyrinth belonged to a larger ritual or symbolic system, whether or not a continuous physical tunnel ever existed.

That distinction allows three different kinds of connection to remain visible:

The physical connection remains unverified. The ritual and symbolic connection, however, can still be examined as an interpretive model: Sphinx as threshold, pyramids as stages of transformation, Labyrinth as ordeal, disorientation and reconstruction.

This does not collapse Hawara into Giza. It asks whether two geographically distinct places could have been understood, in later initiatory readings, as parts of the same sacred map.

Edgar Cayce and the Hall of Records

A change of lens: from this point, the article moves from an interpretive initiatory hypothesis into a visionary / esoteric tradition. The material that follows is historically important to modern Sphinx and Atlantis lore, but it is not archaeological evidence.

Joan Llarch imagines an initiatory geography. Edgar Cayce introduces a different kind of possibility: a repository of memory.

The distinction matters. Cayce’s material belongs to a psychic and esoteric tradition, not to archaeology. It should therefore be read as a modern visionary layer in the history of ideas surrounding Giza, rather than as evidence for an undiscovered chamber.

Yet the correspondence with the questions explored here is striking. In Cayce’s readings, the Sphinx becomes a sentinel associated with a sealed repository containing records of Atlantis and of the movements of its people. The Egyptian repository is described as connected with the Sphinx, while related records are also associated with Bimini/Poseidia and Yucatán.

The central idea is not simply that something was hidden. It is that knowledge was supposedly preserved for a later cycle — deliberately placed beyond the lifetime of the civilization that produced it.

That makes Cayce relevant to the theme of architecture for deep time even if his claims remain outside established archaeology:

  • Llarch asks whether a path of initiation could connect the Sphinx, the pyramids and the Labyrinth.
  • Cayce imagines the Sphinx as guardian of preserved records intended for a future rediscovery.
  • Archaeology asks what structures, passages and chronological relationships can actually be demonstrated.

All three approaches meet at the same threshold, but they are making different kinds of claims.

The attached 1968 volume Edgar Cayce on Atlantis, written by Edgar Evans Cayce under the editorship of Hugh Lynn Cayce, organizes the Atlantis material from Cayce’s life readings into a narrative of repeated destructions, migration, reincarnation and civilizational memory. Within that framework, Atlantis is less useful here as a historical conclusion than as a model of knowledge surviving collapse.

This also creates a useful progression across the two posts:

The Secret of the Sphinx — the Sphinx as threshold to a transformative journey.
Llarch — the threshold extended into an initiatory geography.
Cayce — the threshold extended into a repository of memory for another age.

The question therefore becomes broader than whether a literal Hall of Records exists:

What would a civilization choose to preserve if it believed its own world might not survive?

Before Egypt Was Egypt

The pyramids did not emerge from a cultural vacuum.

Predynastic Egypt extends thousands of years before the Fourth Dynasty, and archaeological material shows that the broader Giza area saw human activity before the construction of the great pyramids.

This matters because it changes a misleading binary:

either
Egypt invented everything suddenly

or
a lost civilization built Egypt

History does not require either extreme.

Knowledge can accumulate.

Techniques can be inherited.

Ritual forms can become monumental.

Older landscapes can acquire new meanings.

The more productive question is therefore:

How much of monumental Egypt was invention, and how much was culmination?

That question leaves room for continuity without requiring an unknown civilization.

It also leaves room for genuine surprise.

Archaeology repeatedly shows that what appears sudden at one scale can reveal long development when the scale is widened.

Atlantis: Answer or Archetype?

Atlantis should enter this discussion carefully.

Plato’s Atlantis is one of the most influential stories of a civilization destroyed by catastrophe. Through later interpretation it became a cultural container for a recurring human possibility:

a civilization before our civilization.

There is no accepted archaeological evidence showing that Atlantis built the Egyptian pyramids, the Osireion or the monuments of Giza.

So Atlantis should not be used here as an answer.

It is more useful as an archetype.

It asks what happens when:

  • knowledge outlives its institutions;
  • memory becomes myth;
  • landscapes are transformed;
  • civilizations inherit fragments whose origins they no longer fully know.

In that sense, the Atlantis question becomes larger than Atlantis itself.

Can knowledge cross a civilizational rupture without preserving the civilization that produced it?

Cayce’s Atlantis: cycles, migration and preserved memory

Cayce’s Atlantis material pushes that question to its extreme. In the readings as collected and interpreted by Edgar Evans Cayce, Atlantis passes through multiple periods of disruption before a final destruction, while groups disperse toward other regions. The material associates those migrations with Egypt and the Americas and repeatedly returns to a moral contrast between knowledge used for integration and knowledge used for domination.

None of this establishes Atlantis archaeologically. But within the intellectual architecture of this post it adds a revealing motif: civilization can disappear while fragments of its knowledge, symbols and moral warnings continue elsewhere.

Read this way, Cayce does not provide the answer to Egypt’s origins. He provides another modern expression of the same deep-time anxiety that surrounds megalithic monuments: the possibility that a civilization could try to send something through a rupture larger than itself.

Now the megalith returns to the centre of the story.

Built to Cross Ages

Imagine designing information for an audience you will never meet.

Language is unstable.

Political institutions are unstable.

Religions change.

Organic media decay.

Digital media, as our own civilization is beginning to discover, depend on extraordinarily fragile layers of infrastructure.

Stone is different.

Geometry is different.

The sky is different.

Together they form three unusually durable media.

Again, this is not evidence that the pyramids were intentionally designed as messages to a post-catastrophe civilization.

It is an observation about the medium.

A geometric relationship remains measurable even after the language used to describe it has disappeared.

A cardinal direction remains.

A celestial cycle can be rediscovered.

A stone can remain where it was placed.

This may be one reason monumental architecture so easily becomes a vessel for memory.

The monument as compressed civilization

A megalithic complex may contain, simultaneously:

engineering
geometry
astronomy
ritual
politics
labor organization
myth
landscape
religion
material science

The civilization disappears.

The monument remains as a compressed object.

Archaeology attempts to decompress it.

That metaphor is particularly useful because decompression is never guaranteed to recover the original file perfectly.

Some information survives.

Some correlations survive without explanation.

Some meaning is irretrievably lost.

And some of what we reconstruct may belong more to us than to the builders.

Time as the Audience

This leads to the question that separates this article from The Secret of the Sphinx.

That article asked about a possible legacy.

This one asks why the architecture itself seems so compatible with extreme duration.

Maybe permanence was simply the natural result of religious and royal ambition.

Maybe the purpose was to maintain cult, kingship and cosmic order indefinitely.

Maybe the monument was intended for the gods rather than for distant human observers.

These possibilities are historically grounded and should come first.

But once a structure survives thousands of years, something strange happens.

Its audience changes.

The builders are gone.

The ritual specialists are gone.

The original spoken explanations are gone.

The monument begins speaking to people who were never part of its culture.

At that point, time itself becomes part of the monument’s meaning.

Not necessarily because its builders consciously chose us.

But because they chose a form capable of reaching us.

What Have We Not Yet Learned to Read?

Modern archaeology has extraordinary instruments.

Muon detectors can reveal density anomalies through hundreds of metres of stone.

Radar can image shallow subsurface contrasts.

Electrical methods can infer resistivity.

Ultrasound can reveal internal structure.

Photogrammetry can preserve surfaces at extraordinary resolution.

AI can correlate datasets at scales that were impractical only a generation ago.

Yet better instruments do not automatically create better interpretation.

The hardest part remains the transition:

measurement
      ↓
structure
      ↓
date
      ↓
function
      ↓
meaning

The first stages increasingly belong to physics and engineering.

The last stages still require history, archaeology, language, comparative evidence and intellectual restraint.

Perhaps that is why Egypt remains so compelling.

We possess technologies the builders could never have imagined, yet the monuments can still place us in the position of beginners.

The message may not be hidden

We often imagine that the great discovery must be behind a wall.

Another chamber.

Another shaft.

Another room.

Another text.

Perhaps one day such a discovery will transform what we know.

But there is another possibility.

Perhaps the information is not hidden inside the monument. Perhaps the monument itself is the information.

Its material.

Its orientation.

Its relationship to landscape.

Its scale.

Its internal sequence.

Its relationship to death and regeneration.

Its resistance to time.

Its continued ability to generate questions.

The deepest unsolved problem may therefore not be another chamber beneath Egypt.

It may be the reading system required to understand what has been visible all along.

As Before, So After

The previous article used the old symbolic movement:

As Above, So Below.

This investigation suggests another axis.

As Before, So After.

The monument stands at the intersection.

Above and below.

Before and after.

Material and meaning.

Evidence and interpretation.

It survives precisely where these opposites meet.

And perhaps that is what makes megalithic Egypt so difficult to exhaust intellectually.

We assume the mystery is how the stones were moved.

That question matters.

But the stones also force another one.

Why choose a form that could remain after almost everything else was gone?

We may discover more chambers.

We may reconstruct more of Hawara.

We may understand the Osireion more completely.

We may find that some spectacular modern claims disappear under better measurement while quieter discoveries transform the field.

But the deepest question may survive all of them.

Why build as if time itself were part of the audience?

And perhaps the greatest discovery still waiting beneath Egypt is not another chamber.

It is learning how to read the monument.
